title: Longest Increasing Subsequence

statement.md: Given a sequence of integers, find the length of its longest strictly increasing subsequence (LIS): the longest sequence of values, in their original order, where each value is strictly greater than the previous one. Equal adjacent values do not extend the subsequence.

This primitive shows up in quantitative work wherever you look for the longest monotone stretch of a signal: longest run of improving quotes, longest accumulation phase in a cumulative return path, or as a subroutine in patience-based matching and alignment algorithms.

Read n and then n integers. Print the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. The intended solution runs in $O(n \log n)$; with n up to 2*10^5 the classic $O(n^2)$ dynamic program is too slow.

statement.title: Strictly vs non-strictly
statement.md: Strictly increasing means each next element must be greater (not equal). For the sequence 4 4 4 the answer is 1, not 3. This single word changes the binary search you use: strict LIS needs lower_bound (first element >= x), while non-strict would use upper_bound (first element > x).

inputFormat: Line 1: the integer n. Line 2: n integers separated by spaces (the sequence, in order).
outputFormat: One integer: the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
constraints: An O(n^2) solution will not fit the time limit; aim for O(n log n).

examples.explanation: One longest strictly increasing subsequence is 2 3 7 18 (also 2 5 7 101 or 2 5 7 18): length 4.
1 2 4 5 (or 1 3 4 5) is strictly increasing with length 4; no length-5 subsequence exists.

hints: Maintain an array tails: tails[k] is the smallest possible tail value of any strictly increasing subsequence of length k+1 seen so far.
tails is always sorted in increasing order, so for each new value x you can binary-search for the first entry >= x (bisect_left / lower_bound).

If x is greater than every tail it extends the longest subsequence (append it); otherwise it replaces the first tail that is >= x, a strictly smaller tail for that length, which can only help future extensions. The answer is the final length of tails.

solutions.python:
import sys
from bisect import bisect_left


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()
    n = int(data[0])
    tails = []
    for s in data[1:1 + n]:
        x = int(s)
        i = bisect_left(tails, x)
        if i == len(tails):
            tails.append(x)
        else:
            tails[i] = x
    print(len(tails))


main()
